## Measurable Functions

Measurable functions are the structure-preserving maps of measure theory, in
the same way that continuous functions are the structure-preserving maps of
[[topology]] and linear maps are those of [[linear-algebra]]. They are the
functions we are able to integrate (see [[lebesgue-integral]]), and in
probability theory they are the **random variables**.

The central idea is that a measure assigns a size or a probability to
*subsets*, not to points, and only to subsets in a chosen
[[sigma-algebra|$\sigma$-algebra]]. A function $f$ transports the question
"how large is $A$?" about a set $A$ in its codomain into the question "how
large is $f^{-1}(A)$?" about a set in its domain. This only makes sense when
$f^{-1}(A)$ is itself in the $\sigma$-algebra of the domain.

## Definition

:::{.definition data-title="Measurable Function"}

Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{G})$ be measurable spaces. A function
$f:X\to Y$ is **$(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})$-measurable** if

$$
f^{-1}(B) := \{x\in X : f(x)\in B\} \in \mathcal{F}
\qquad\text{for all } B\in\mathcal{G}.
$$

:::

When the $\sigma$-algebras are clear we simply say that $f$ is **measurable**,
or **$\mathcal{F}$-measurable**. If the codomain is $\mathbb{R}$ (or
$\mathbb{R}^n$), it carries the [[borel-sigma-algebra|Borel
$\sigma$-algebra]] $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}$ by default, so that a function
$f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathcal{F}$-measurable if
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$.

The definition is the exact analogue of continuity, with $\sigma$-algebras in
place of topologies: a function is continuous if preimages of open sets are
open, and measurable if preimages of measurable sets are measurable.

Two special cases of this definition appear often.

- If $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces, $f$ is **Borel measurable** if it is
  $(\mathcal{B}_X,\mathcal{B}_Y)$-measurable.
- A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is **Lebesgue measurable** if it is
  $(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$-measurable, where
  $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets.
  Since $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}\subsetneq\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}$, every Borel
  measurable function is Lebesgue measurable, but not conversely.

### Pushforward Measures

If $f:(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)\to(Y,\mathcal{G})$ is measurable, then
$\mu\circ f^{-1}$ is well defined on $\mathcal{G}$, and is a measure on $Y$
called the **pushforward** (or **image**) measure,

$$
(f_*\mu)(B) = \mu\left(f^{-1}(B)\right), \qquad B\in\mathcal{G}.
$$

Measurability is exactly the condition that makes this transport possible.
For example, let $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}$ be the outcomes of a die and let
$f(\omega)=+10$ if $\omega$ is odd and $-10$ if $\omega$ is even, the payoff of
a bet. Then $f_*\mathbb{P}(\{10\})=\mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(10))=\mathbb{P}(\{1,3,5\})$,
and the probability of losing money is $\mathbb{P}(f^{-1}((-\infty,0)))$.

## Random Variables

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a [[probability-spaces|probability
space]].

:::{.definition data-title="Random Variable"}

A **random variable** is an $\mathcal{F}$-measurable function
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^n$, in which case $X$ is a random
vector).

:::

See [[random-variables]]. Measurability is what allows us to speak of the
probability of events defined by $X$: the set $\{X\le x\}=X^{-1}((-\infty,x])$
is in $\mathcal{F}$ for every $x$, so $\mathbb{P}(X\le x)$ is defined. The
pushforward measure of $\mathbb{P}$ is the **distribution** (or **law**) of
$X$,

$$
\mu_X(B) = \mathbb{P}(X\in B) = \mathbb{P}\left(X^{-1}(B)\right),
\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}.
$$

Further connections with probability theory:

- **Generated $\sigma$-algebra.** The collection
  $\sigma(X)=\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}\}$ is the smallest
  $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ for which $X$ is measurable, and records the
  information in $X$ (see [[generated-sigma-algebra]]). A random variable $X$
  is $\mathcal{G}$-measurable if and only if $\sigma(X)\subseteq\mathcal{G}$.
- **Functions of random variables.** If $X$ is a random variable and $g$ is
  Borel measurable, then $g(X)$ is a random variable, by the composition
  result below. This includes all continuous $g$.
- **Doob-Dynkin lemma.** A random variable $Y$ is $\sigma(X)$-measurable if
  and only if $Y=g(X)$ for some Borel measurable function $g$. This says that
  the information in $X$ determines exactly the functions of $X$.
- **Expectation.** The expectation of $X$ is the Lebesgue integral
  $\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb{P}$, which is defined for measurable
  functions, and satisfies $\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\int g\,d\mu_X$.
- **Stochastic processes.** A process $(X_t)$ is **adapted** to a filtration
  $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ if each $X_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable (see
  [[filtrations-and-adapted-processes]]), and a conditional expectation
  $\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$ is by definition $\mathcal{G}$-measurable
  (see [[conditional-expectation-random-variables]]).

## Equivalent Conditions

It is enough to check measurability on a family that generates the
$\sigma$-algebra of the codomain.

:::{.theorem data-title="Generating Sets"}

Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{G})$ be measurable spaces, where
$\mathcal{G}=\sigma(\mathcal{E})$ is generated by a collection $\mathcal{E}$.
Then $f:X\to Y$ is $(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})$-measurable if and only if
$f^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal{F}$ for all $E\in\mathcal{E}$.

:::

:::{.proof}
The only if direction is immediate since $\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$.
For the converse, the collection
$$
\mathcal{A}=\{B\subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}\}
$$
is a $\sigma$-algebra, because preimages commute with complements and
countable unions, and $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under both. It contains
$\mathcal{E}$ by assumption, so it contains $\sigma(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{G}$.
:::

For real-valued functions this gives several equivalent conditions.

:::{.theorem data-title="Equivalent Conditions for Real-Valued Functions"}

For a measurable space $(X,\mathcal{F})$ and a function $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ the
following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is $\mathcal{F}$-measurable;
2. $f^{-1}((a,\infty))\in\mathcal{F}$ for all $a\in\mathbb{R}$;
3. $f^{-1}([a,\infty))\in\mathcal{F}$ for all $a\in\mathbb{R}$;
4. $f^{-1}((-\infty,a))\in\mathcal{F}$ for all $a\in\mathbb{R}$;
5. $f^{-1}((-\infty,a])\in\mathcal{F}$ for all $a\in\mathbb{R}$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Condition 1 implies each of 2 to 5, since rays are Borel sets. Conversely, the
open rays $(a,\infty)$ generate $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}$: from them we get
$(-\infty,b]=(b,\infty)^c$, then $(a,b]=(a,\infty)\cap(-\infty,b]$ and
$(a,b)=\bigcup_n(a,b-\tfrac1n]$, and every open set is a countable union of
open intervals. The same holds for the other three families, since each is
obtained from another by complements or countable intersections and unions,
for example $[a,\infty)=\bigcap_n(a-\tfrac1n,\infty)$. The result follows from
the generating sets theorem.
:::

The same conditions characterize measurability of functions into the extended
reals $[-\infty,\infty]$, which is needed for suprema and limits. A function
$f=(f_1,\dots,f_n):X\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is measurable if and only if each
component $f_i$ is, since $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ is the
[[product-sigma-algebra|product $\sigma$-algebra]] of $n$ copies of
$\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}$.

## Important Results

:::{.theorem data-title="Composition"}

If $f:(X,\mathcal{F})\to(Y,\mathcal{G})$ and $g:(Y,\mathcal{G})\to(Z,\mathcal{H})$
are measurable, then $g\circ f$ is $(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{H})$-measurable.

:::

:::{.proof}
For $C\in\mathcal{H}$, $(g\circ f)^{-1}(C)=f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C))$. Here
$g^{-1}(C)\in\mathcal{G}$ and so $f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C))\in\mathcal{F}$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Continuous Functions are Borel Measurable"}

Every continuous function $f:X\to Y$ between topological spaces is Borel
measurable.

:::

:::{.proof}
By the generating sets theorem it suffices to check the open sets, which
generate $\mathcal{B}_Y$. If $U\subseteq Y$ is open then $f^{-1}(U)$ is open
by continuity, hence in $\mathcal{B}_X$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Algebra of Measurable Functions"}

If $f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}$ are $\mathcal{F}$-measurable and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, then
$cf$, $f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$ are measurable. If
$g\neq0$, then $f/g$ is measurable.

:::

:::{.proof}
For the sum, note that $f(x)+g(x)>a$ if and only if there is a rational $q$
with $f(x)>q$ and $g(x)>a-q$, so
$$
\{f+g>a\} = \bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}}\{f>q\}\cap\{g>a-q\}\in\mathcal{F}.
$$
The remaining cases follow from the composition theorem, since $f\mapsto cf$
and $f\mapsto|f|$ are continuous, and from
$fg=\tfrac14\left((f+g)^2-(f-g)^2\right)$ and
$\max(f,g)=\tfrac12\left(f+g+|f-g|\right)$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Limits of Measurable Functions"}

If $f_n:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ are $\mathcal{F}$-measurable, $n\ge1$, then
$\sup_nf_n$, $\inf_nf_n$, $\limsup_nf_n$ and $\liminf_nf_n$ are measurable.
In particular, if $f_n\to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

:::

:::{.proof}
We have $\{\sup_nf_n>a\}=\bigcup_n\{f_n>a\}\in\mathcal{F}$, so the supremum is
measurable, and $\inf_nf_n=-\sup_n(-f_n)$. Then
$\limsup_nf_n=\inf_{k}\sup_{n\ge k}f_n$ and
$\liminf_nf_n=\sup_{k}\inf_{n\ge k}f_n$ are measurable, and when the limit
exists it equals the $\limsup$.
:::

The last result is a key difference from continuity: pointwise limits of
continuous functions need not be continuous, but pointwise limits of
measurable functions are always measurable.

:::{.theorem data-title="Approximation by Simple Functions"}

A **simple function** is a measurable function taking finitely many values.
Every measurable $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is the pointwise limit of an increasing
sequence of non-negative simple functions $0\le s_1\le s_2\le\dots$. If $f$ is
bounded the convergence is uniform. Every measurable real function is a
difference of two such limits, $f=f^+-f^-$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Define

$$
s_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n2^n-1}\frac{k}{2^n}\,
\mathbf{1}_{\{k2^{-n}\le f<(k+1)2^{-n}\}} + n\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f\ge n\}}.
$$

Each set in the sum is the preimage of an interval, so it is in $\mathcal{F}$
and $s_n$ is simple. Refining the grid from $n$ to $n+1$ rounds $f$ down to a
finer level, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}\le f$, and $f-s_n\le2^{-n}$ wherever
$f<n$, which gives $s_n\uparrow f$.
:::

This result is how the [[lebesgue-integral]] is constructed: the integral is
defined first for simple functions (see [[calculus-of-simple-functions]]) and
then extended to measurable functions by this approximation and the
[[monotone-convergence-theorem]].

## Examples

1. **Constant functions** are measurable for every $\sigma$-algebra, since
   $f^{-1}(B)$ is either $\emptyset$ or $X$.

2. **Indicator functions.** For $A\subseteq X$, the indicator
   $\mathbf{1}_A$ is $\mathcal{F}$-measurable if and only if $A\in\mathcal{F}$,
   because $\mathbf{1}_A^{-1}(B)$ is one of $\emptyset$, $A$, $A^c$ or $X$.
   Simple functions are finite linear combinations of indicators.

3. **Extreme choices of $\sigma$-algebra.** If $\mathcal{F}=\{\emptyset,X\}$
   is the trivial $\sigma$-algebra, the only measurable real functions are the
   constants. If $\mathcal{F}=2^X$ is the power set, every function is
   measurable. This is why every function on a finite probability space with
   the power set is a random variable.

4. **A function that is not measurable.** On $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}$ with
   $\mathcal{F}=\{\emptyset,\{1,3,5\},\{2,4,6\},\Omega\}$ (we can only observe
   whether the roll is odd or even), the function $X(\omega)=\omega$ is not
   $\mathcal{F}$-measurable, since $X^{-1}(\{1\})=\{1\}\notin\mathcal{F}$. The
   parity $\mathbf{1}_{\{\text{odd}\}}$ is measurable.

5. **Continuous functions** such as $f(x)=x^2$ and $f(x)=e^x$ are Borel
   measurable, and so are all polynomials and $\sin$, $\cos$, by the continuity
   theorem above.

6. **Monotone functions.** If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is non-decreasing
   then $\{f>a\}$ is an interval for every $a$, so $f$ is Borel measurable even
   if it has countably many jumps, such as the floor function.

7. **The Dirichlet function** $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is nowhere continuous,
   but is Borel measurable because $\mathbb{Q}$ is a countable union of
   points and hence Borel. It is the pointwise limit
   $\lim_m\lim_n\cos^{2n}(m!\pi x)$ of continuous functions.

8. **Non-measurable functions** exist but need the axiom of choice. If
   $V\subset[0,1]$ is a Vitali set, then $\mathbf{1}_V$ is not Lebesgue
   measurable. See [[vitalli-non-measurability-theorem]].

9. **Stock prices.** If $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ models a financial
   market and $S_T=S_0\exp\left((\mu-\frac12\sigma^2)T+\sigma W_T\right)$, then
   $S_T$ is a random variable, as a continuous function of the random variable
   $W_T$. So are payoffs such as $(S_T-K)^+$, as continuous functions of $S_T$.
